case_study_insert.main_stem: Harbourview Pharmacy (HVP) is a public limited company in the retail pharmacy and consumer health sector, employing a workforce of 120. Founded in 1998 by Margaret Chen, it runs 18 high-street branches and operates an autocratic leadership style within a flat structure. HVP plans to invest $950,000 in automated dispensing robots and a click-and-collect e-commerce platform, financed by a $550,000 ten-year bank loan, $250,000 retained profit and a $150,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $18 a unit and a selling price of $58 for a prescription or OTC item, and currently dispenses 25,000 units a year. HVP faces two problems: a 2.7% dispensing error rate and rising complaints about a 9.6-minute counter wait.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Service Report — Q3 2025: HVP dispensed 6,200 prescription and OTC units last month with a 2.7% dispensing error rate, up from 1.6% a year earlier. Customer complaints about queue times rose from 48 to 77 per month. Average wait at the counter is 9.6 minutes. A survey of 1,000 shoppers found that 66% would use click-and-collect if it cut waiting time, and 54% buy more when staff offer health advice. 18 of 120 pharmacy staff have not completed on-the-job training on the automated dispensing robots; a vendor course costs $640 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Harbourview Pharmacy for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as HVP's $550,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.8% from $12.90 to $13.78 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for pharmacy and counter staff. (3) Wholesale medicine and PPE input costs have risen 9.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on over-the-counter health products grew 4.6% over the same period.

questions.question_text: HVP is funding its $950,000 automation programme with a $550,000 bank loan, $250,000 retained profit and a $150,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HVP of using the $150,000 share issue rather than increasing the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share issue proceeds are equity that require no interest or repayment, so HVP avoids adding debt service to the $550,000 loan while meeting fixed costs of $600,000 a year. The $150,000 can be spent on the click-and-collect e-commerce platform and on cutting the 9.6-minute counter wait, rather than being paid to a lender as finance charges on the $950,000 programme.

Point 2: Equity improves resilience if the 2.7% dispensing error rate forces costly rework and revenue falls below the current 25,000 units, because there is no fixed repayment that could strain liquidity. It also spreads the risk of the 18-branch automation across new shareholders rather than leaving the company wholly exposed to the bank. A larger loan would require repayments whether or not click-and-collect reduces the 77 monthly complaints, whereas equity gives HVP time to embed the robots. New shareholders may also bring retail property experience useful when rolling click-and-collect out to all 18 branches.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to HVP's expansion, complaints and costs.

questions.question_text: HVP's queue-time complaints rose from 48 to 77 a month. Consider a click-and-collect e-commerce platform, recruiting part-time counter staff, or self-service collection lockers. Which should HVP choose to cut the 9.6-minute wait? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Click-and-collect e-commerce platform: Allowing customers to order online and skip the queue directly addresses the 9.6-minute wait, and the survey of 1,000 shoppers found 66% would use it. It also supports the $950,000 automation programme and gathers useful data, but it needs IT investment and will not help customers who still want face-to-face advice from the 54% who buy more after such advice.

Recruiting part-time counter staff: Extra staff could open more lanes and cut the 77 monthly complaints quickly, but they add to fixed costs of $600,000 a year and require training on the dispensing robots, especially as 18 of 120 staff still need on-the-job training. With a 2.7% error rate, rushed new staff could make accuracy worse.

Self-service collection lockers: Lockers let customers collect pre-packed items at any time and reduce counter pressure without ongoing wages. They complement the robots and can be placed in all 18 branches, but the upfront cost adds to the $950,000 programme, and some older customers may avoid them, limiting the reduction in the 9.6-minute wait.

Ordering online also gives HVP data on the 66% of surveyed shoppers who want shorter waits, helping it measure whether the 9.6-minute queue actually falls.

Recommendation: HVP should choose the click-and-collect e-commerce platform, with lockers added later at busy branches. It matches the 66% of surveyed shoppers, uses the automation already being funded and cuts the wait without permanent staffing costs. Extra counter staff are rejected because they raise fixed costs and risk the 2.7% error rate; lockers alone are rejected because they do not serve customers seeking advice and add upfront cost.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the options with minimal reference to HVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HVP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why extra staff and lockers alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: HVP combines autocratic leadership with a flat structure. Explain two benefits for HVP of this approach in reducing its 2.7% dispensing error rate and 77 monthly complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership lets Margaret Chen impose strict, uniform dispensing checks across all 18 branches, which is important when the error rate has risen from 1.6% to 2.7%. Clear rules can be enforced immediately, protecting customers and reducing the 77 monthly complaints, while the 54% of shoppers who value staff advice still receive a consistent service.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so warnings about errors or queue problems reach senior managers quickly from the 120 staff. Faster decisions help tackle the 9.6-minute counter wait and let HVP respond to the 66% of surveyed shoppers who want click-and-collect, protecting the $58 selling price and the $40 contribution on each of the 25,000 units dispensed. The combination is useful with 18 branches: strict rules keep the 2.7% error rate visible while short reporting lines let branch staff escalate the 9.6-minute queue before it becomes another complaint. That matters because Margaret Chen cannot supervise every counter personally.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HVP's errors, complaints and service data.

questions.question_text: HVP must train 18 of 120 pharmacy staff on the automated dispensing robots. Consider on-the-job training or a vendor course costing $640 per employee. Which should HVP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside the robots is directly relevant to HVP's own equipment, costs no fees, and keeps all 18 staff dispensing the 25,000 units a year, which matters while the 9.6-minute counter wait and 77 monthly complaints already strain branches. It also lets experienced pharmacists demonstrate checks that reduce the 2.7% error rate. The drawbacks are that trainers are working staff whose output falls, standards can vary across 18 branches, and no certificate is awarded.

Vendor course: At $640 per employee, certifying all 18 costs $11,520 (18 × $640), small against the $950,000 automation programme. It gives structured technical training and a recognised certificate that supports quality assurance, and removes staff from busy counters so learning is uninterrupted. However, it takes 18 of 120 staff away from branches temporarily, which could worsen the 9.6-minute wait, and generic content may need on-site follow-up to match HVP's robots.

Accuracy is the central judgement: with a 2.7% dispensing error rate and 18 staff still untrained, factory-style practice on the robots could embed safe checking habits immediately, whereas a classroom certificate proves knowledge but not safe dispensing at the counter. The $11,520 fee is affordable beside $950,000, but time away from branches would show up in the 77 monthly complaints.

Decision: HVP should choose on-the-job training first, adding short vendor certification for lead pharmacists later. On-the-job training protects dispensing capacity when queues are already long, is free and is robot-specific; full vendor training is rejected because removing 18 staff would deepen the 77-complaint problem and the $11,520 fee duplicates skills best learned at the counter.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to HVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of HVP's queues and costs.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and technical relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HVP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($58 − $18) = $600,000 ÷ $40 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $58 − $18 = $40. Answer: contribution per unit is $40.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HVP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 15,000-unit break-even output with 25,000 units dispensed shows a margin of safety of 10,000 units, giving room to automate all 18 branches.
2. Contribution of $40 a unit lets managers model the effect of the 66% of 1,000 surveyed shoppers who would use click-and-collect; retaining the $58 price while cutting the 9.6-minute wait protects that contribution.
3. With fixed costs of $600,000 and contribution of $40, managers can set the dispensing volume needed to service the $550,000 loan before extending the $950,000 programme.
4. Average total cost ($600,000 ÷ 25,000 + $18 = $42) can be benchmarked quarterly to detect waste from the 2.7% error rate and to judge whether the 9.4% medicine input inflation is being controlled.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $40 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 25,000-unit output; click-and-collect demand modelling; loan-service volume for the $550,000 loan; and average total cost of $42 to monitor errors and input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HVP's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has HVP's performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 38.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 13.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024: 1,400 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = 35.0%; 400 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = 10.0%; 400 ÷ 2,500 × 100 = 16.0%. 2025: 1,900 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 38.0%; 650 ÷ 5,000 × 100 = 13.0%; 650 ÷ 3,250 × 100 = 20.0%. Revenue grew to $5,000,000 while cost of sales rose to $3,100,000, so the first margin widened; operating profit reached $650,000. Capital employed increased to $3,250,000, yet the return on that larger base improved, and interest payable fell from $80,000 to $70,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The rise from 35.0% to 38.0% shows HVP is controlling the cost of medicines and OTC stock despite 9.4% input inflation. The move from 10.0% to 13.0% indicates fixed costs of $600,000 are being spread over more of the 25,000 units, helped by lower interest charges. The return on capital employed rising from 16.0% to 20.0% is the strongest evidence because it shows the enlarged $3,250,000 asset base is generating more profit, which supports the $950,000 automation programme. A limitation is that no cash or receivables are shown, so better profitability does not prove HVP can meet short-term debts; the $550,000 loan still requires repayment.

Conclusion: HVP's performance has improved. Every measure rose, and the 20.0% return on capital employed confirms that the larger asset base is creating value rather than simply increasing sales revenue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate percentage calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HVP of introducing click-and-collect to cut the 9.6-minute counter wait.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 1,000 shoppers found that 66% would use click-and-collect if it cut waiting time, so the service could attract customers away from rivals and raise the 25,000 units dispensed without changing the $58 selling price. Faster collection would reduce the 77 monthly complaints and free pharmacists to give the advice that 54% of shoppers say encourages extra purchases, lifting the $40 contribution on each unit.

Disadvantage: setting up click-and-collect adds to the $950,000 automation spend and to fixed costs of $600,000 a year, and it will not help customers who lack internet access or still expect face-to-face service. If the 2.7% dispensing error rate is not reduced first, pre-packed orders could be wrong when collected, turning a queue-time improvement into a new source of complaints. HVP should pilot the service in a few high-footfall branches and compare complaint counts before extending it across all 18. That keeps the $950,000 spend focused on sites where the 9.6-minute wait is worst.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to HVP's survey, contribution and service problems.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.8% minimum wage increase and the 9.4% rise in medicine input costs will affect HVP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): If HVP's $550,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $550,000 = $4,125 a year (0.0075 × $550,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $600,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the effect is zero. Higher rates may also make future borrowing for the $950,000 automation dearer, but HVP can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.8%, to $13.78 an hour): With a workforce of 120 across 18 branches, this raises wage bills for pharmacy and counter staff and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual wage total can be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 25,000 units ÷ 120 staff = 208.3 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if output per worker holds or grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $40 contribution per unit is squeezed while the 9.6-minute wait persists.

Medicine input costs (9.4%): The $18 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound can be calculated: if the whole variable cost rose 9.4% it would add 0.094 × $18 = $1.69 per unit; at 25,000 units that is $42,300 a year. This erodes the $40 contribution on every prescription and OTC item, and the 2.7% error rate adds waste, though 4.6% growth in OTC spending and the click-and-collect service give some pricing and volume offset.

Conclusion: The 9.4% rise in medicine input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 25,000 units and directly attacks the $40 contribution that funds the $950,000 programme, with errors amplifying it; the interest rise costs only $4,125 a year and the wage effect, though real, cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and higher OTC demand.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to HVP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on HVP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
